newsitem.title: DUBAI: A U.S. plane deal seen angering Saudi militants.
newsitem.headline: A U.S. plane deal seen angering Saudi militants.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is shopping for a new generation of U.S. fighters but a purchase could deepen the hostility of Moslem militants opposed to the Saudi royal family and its close American allies.
"If this goes ahead it will add a lot to the accumulating resentment," Saad al-Fagih, London-based leader of the Movement for Islamic Reform in Arabia, said.
"The militants are already moving in a violent direction. They will say that the Americans and Saudis are looting the country. The aircraft would provide them with logic," he added.

The United States said last week that key ally Saudi Arabia was shopping for fighters but Washington reacted cautiously to a report that Riyadh would buy up to 100 Lockheed Martin Corp F-16s in a deal that could be worth up to $10 billion.
A major U.S. arms package could be politically sensitive for Saudi Arabia's rulers after two bombings killed 24 Americans in seven months.

"Militants are already angered by Americans walking the streets, never mind a deal like this," said a Western diplomat based in Riyadh. "I don't think you need to ask them how they would feel about a plane deal with Americans. They have already made it clear."
The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia last month warned Americans it continued to receive unconfirmed reports of possible attacks on U.S. interests in the kingdom and urged them be cautious.

Moslem militant rage has been brewing in Saudi Arabia since the 1991 Gulf War, when zealots watched half a million mostly U.S. soldiers land on Saudi soil to launch an attack on Iraqi troops occupying Kuwait.
Loosely organised underground groups condemn the al-Saud royal family as subservient to Washington and a high-profile fighter plane contract could fan their anger, Saudi analysts said.
Militants have been blamed and beheaded for one of the bombings and the Saudi authorities are still investigating the second blast in Dhahran last June 25.
U.S. officials last month accused the Saudis of a lack of cooperation in a joint probe into the blast, a charge that has strained ties between Washington and Riyadh.
A fighter package would help ease tensions between the two governments, analysts said.

Saudi Arabia, one of Washington's staunchest Middle East allies, already has a variety of U.S. arms on order worth $25 billion until the end of the century and also has a huge arsenal of European weapons.

"This would improve ties and pave the way for Saudi Arabia to get more sophisticated weapons from the Americans," said a Saudi-based defence industry executive. "But on the other hand, there has been unrest in the kingdom."
Some Saudi analysts question the wisdom of a possible deal -- with a price tag estimated between $2.5 billion and $10 billion -- when the days of easy oil money are over.
"This is mind boggling. Is it really needed? They could spend it on education, development and hospitals," said one.
Washington said Saudi Arabia was seeking to replace its ageing fleet of 114 F-5 fighters.
Saudi Arabia is not alone. Other Gulf Arab states, suspicious of regional powers Iran and Iraq, are pumping billions of dollars into state-of-the-art weaponry.
But analysts seriously doubt they could defend themselves against a major attack without American help.
"Why do we need all these planes when the American army is going to come to the rescue before we even get off the ground?" said the Saudi analyst.
